alt: The reflective paper is worth 10 of the Team Project’s 40 marks, beside 30 for the presentation, with a maximum of 800 words assessed entirely on AO2. Its two strands are the effectiveness of the collaboration and the candidate’s learning, including changed personal views.
caption: Reflect on the process, not the findings: teamwork is assessed only here.

alt: Seven aspects to evaluate, each with guiding questions: agreeing the problem, allocating perspectives, communication, decision-making, handling disagreement, organisation and your own role. All are judged against the team’s goal rather than how pleasant the work felt.
caption: Effectiveness means progress towards the team’s goal, not a pleasant time.

alt: General claims such as “communication was sometimes a problem” and “communicate better” set against specific ones: two members researched the same council report in week three because sources were not allocated, so the team should have kept a shared list of who covers which sources.
caption: Name a specific moment, then an improvement someone could act on.

alt: Four areas of learning: the problem itself, research skills, presentation skills, and changes to personal views shaped by teammates’ perspectives. Two areas explored in depth with examples beat four that are only listed.
caption: Choose two areas of learning and explore them, rather than listing four.

alt: Four moves in each paragraph: what happened, what it shows about the team or you, how effective it was against the team’s goal or your learning, and what you would do differently. A bar shows description as the smallest share of the paragraph.
caption: Keep description short; most words go on meaning, effect and change.

alt: An 800-word plan: context 60 to 80 words, effectiveness of collaboration 300 to 350, improvements 100 to 120, learning and changed views 200 to 250, and a closing judgement 40 to 60.
caption: Spend the words on the two assessed strands.

after: ## Worked example: weak and strong paragraphs
alt: The weak paragraph makes only general claims about teamwork and learning. The strong learning paragraph moves from a specific event, a teammate’s interviews about stallholders paying by the hour, to what it shows, how it changed the writer’s solution, and a new habit of checking who produced a source.
caption: Specific event, what it shows, its effect, what changes: in every paragraph.
